props.title: In Your Hands

sections.content: In Your Hands represents a pivotal entry in the Dogme 95 movement, though it arrived after the strict adherence to the manifesto had softened. Like Breaking the Waves (1996) and The Celebration (1998), it tackles faith and morality in modern Denmark, but through a uniquely female perspective. Director Annette K. Olesen crafts a prison drama that explores the tension between religious belief and secular rationality, echoing themes found in Doubt (2008) but with the raw, handheld aesthetic characteristic of Danish cinema from this period.

sections.content: The film's exploration of faith healing and institutional power dynamics recalls other powerful prison dramas like Dead Man Walking (1995) and Monster (2003), but with a distinctly European art house sensibility. Ann Eleonora Jørgensen's performance as the prison chaplain Anna brings to mind Emily Watson's role in Breaking the Waves (1996), both wrestling with questions of faith versus reality in increasingly challenging circumstances.

The film's visual style, while influenced by Dogme 95, shows how the movement evolved beyond its initial rigid rules. Like Italian for Beginners (2000) and Open Hearts (2002), it maintains the movement's emphasis on natural lighting and location shooting while allowing for more conventional dramatic techniques. The prison setting creates a pressure cooker environment similar to A Prophet (2009), where faith, power, and redemption intersect. SUBHEAD: Faith and Morality in Contemporary Cinema

sections.content: In Your Hands sits within a broader tradition of films examining spiritual crisis in modern institutions, alongside works like Silent Light (2007) and Of Gods and Men (2010). The prison setting amplifies these themes, creating a microcosm where faith and skepticism clash daily. Trine Dyrholm's portrayal of the mysterious inmate Kate echoes other complex female characters in Danish cinema, particularly those in Antichrist (2009) and The Commune (2016).
